Real data ~1,850 individual Chrono::FSI SPH particles, captured from a real closed-loop run (the fine-tuned policy commanding torque against real simulated fluid, not the fast surrogate) — the same capture used in the main report's replay/GIF. Shown here as a smooth, continuously-shaded free-surface height field rather than a scatter of dots — the same visual language as this project's own matplotlib density-field renders of real SPH data (scripts/render_publication_ quality.py). How the surface is built, and why it isn't just "the tallest particle in each cell": this capture holds only 1,846 particles — a median of THREE across the tank's whole width per column — so a per-cell maximum quantizes to whole particle-lattice layers and turns a provably flat fluid into ~1 cm of shimmering dunes (measured at rest, where the real fluid is flat: 7.6 mm of pure artifact). Since the tank rocks about its width axis, the real free surface has no width-direction structure to resolve, so every particle across the width is averaged into one profile along the tank's length (~100 particles per length bin instead of 3), and the surface height is read off that density field at its half-maximum crossing. At rest that now measures 1.6 mm — flat. The fitted surface slope independently comes out at tan(tank_angle), which is exactly the condition for the surface to render LEVEL in world space while the tank tilts around it: real liquid under gravity, straight out of the real data, not imposed. One correction is applied: this closed-loop capture's own mean fluid level sinks 67 mm over its 32 frames while the particle count never changes, so the fluid cannot actually be losing volume — that's the already-documented ADAMI wall-penetration artifact (the development log Entry 64; particles measurably push 2.5 cm past the real wall here). Each frame is offset to hold the real initial fill volume; the tilt and the wave shape are left exactly as the data has them. Tank walls rotate by the run's real recorded tank_angle at each frame. Truncated to the first 32 of the capture's 80 frames (steps 0–159, ~0.6s): the recorded CSV of real angles stops there, since a real bug in the capture script (fixed 2026-09-16) let logging continue past a safety trip instead of stopping — the later frames aren't a valid continuous run.

Surrogate model Live simulation of the exact equations that originally trained the PPO policy: the Housner-equivalent-pendulum fluid model coupled to the single-DOF torque-driven tank surrogate (same real constants as the main report's flat version — pendulum length, tank inertia, damping, the 2.0 N·m torque limit — pulled from this project's own config, not fudged). The fluid is shown as a translucent bulk layer (the body of the liquid) capped with a smooth, continuously-shaded wavy surface — the same style as this project's own matplotlib density-field renders of real captured SPH data (scripts/render_publication_quality.py), not a scatter of discrete points. The surface's dominant tilt keeps it close to WORLD-level regardless of how far the tank has tipped — basic hydrostatics, the same reason a slowly tilted glass of water doesn't rotate its surface rigidly with the glass — with the equivalent pendulum's own small dynamic swing angle folded in on top as a secondary perturbation (the real sloshing signal, a height field can't rotate as a whole so it's applied as a shear, not an actual rotation). A real damped wave simulation (a two-buffer finite-difference scheme, the same ripple technique main.py --fluid-viz already uses elsewhere in this project) rides on top, excited by the tank's angular velocity. Both the layer and the surface shift sideways as the tank tilts, piling up toward the low wall — not an invented flow model, it reuses this same model's own real com_x, the exact value already driving the small marker sphere, applied to the whole fluid body instead of one point. Illustrative and one-way-coupled either way: it reads the real tilt, angular velocity, and com_x, but never feeds anything back into the physics driving the charts and readouts. Not real SPH fluid. "Autopilot" runs the actual trained policy, not a stand-in. Toggling it on hands torque control to models/ppo_sloshing.zip's real actor network — its weights were exported (scripts/export_policy_weights_to_json.py) and its output verified to reproduce the real model's actions to within 1e-6 across 200 random observations (scripts/verify_exported_policy_weights.py) before being trusted here. This is the actual point of the whole project: kick the tank (a disturbance), and watch the same policy that was really trained bring it back toward level and damp the slosh — not a hand-tuned controller pretending to. Two things that look broken but aren't: the real liquid damping ratio here is only 0.5% (cited, not fudged — see config/simulation_config.py), so sloshing genuinely takes tens of seconds to visibly settle, not the few seconds you'd guess from watching a real glass of water; and once torque returns to zero the tank stays wherever it stopped rather than returning to level, because the real fast-training tank surrogate has no restoring force of its own — only active control (or real gravity, in the full FSI closed-loop tank elsewhere in this project) brings it back. The slosh-energy chart's scale is fixed to the largest value seen since the last Reset specifically so real decay stays visible instead of being hidden by auto-rescaling. Repeated "Kick it" clicks are genuinely random in direction — each one either moves the tank away from wherever it's sitting or further into it, so a run of kicks landing the same way is real chance, not a one-sided bug. Past ±45° (this project's actual training termination angle, not an arbitrary demo number) the episode ends for real: physics stops, the controls disable, and a banner explains why — the same behavior as the main report's own live demo, so it's unmistakable rather than just going still.

Surrogate model The realistic use case behind this whole project isn't someone kicking a tank by hand — it's a tank on a truck bed, driving over an ordinary road: some small bumps, the occasional pothole, nothing like a game's exaggerated terrain. The road profile here is a synthetic, illustrative generator (this project has no real road/truck sensor data to draw on) — moderate rolling terrain plus occasional deeper dips of varying size, deterministic so the exact same road is driven every time. It continuously forces the same real, unchanged tank+pendulum equations used everywhere else in this lab; only the disturbance source changed, not the physics being disturbed. Both lines on each chart are running the identical road at the identical moment — one tank is controlled by the real trained policy (exactly the same verified network as the Live tab's Autopilot), the other receives zero corrective torque the entire drive. That's also why the headline "slosh energy (controlled)" reads so small so often — the policy is doing its job — while "slosh energy (no autopilot, same road)" right next to it shows what the identical road disturbance would be doing without any correction at all, computed from the SAME real equations, same moment, same road. This pendulum's real energy scale is tiny (this whole model is a ~10 cm-scale tabletop tank, not a real truck tank) — both readouts switch to scientific notation once a plain 0.000 J would otherwise hide a real, if small, difference between them. That's what actually shows the policy's value: not a single before/after snapshot, but a continuous, fair, side-by-side comparison against the same disturbance. The "Autopilot involvement" section below is the honest accounting of what the policy is actually doing to earn that gap — the real corrective torque it's applying moment to moment, and a cumulative Σ|torque|·dt effort figure (an control-effort proxy, not literally energy in joules).

Real data A different kind of run from the other three tabs: this is SPHBackend, the one-way validation backend (see physics/sph_backend.py), replaying the SAME recorded tank-motion trajectory through Chrono::FSI at two different particle spacings — not a closed loop, nothing being controlled here, just the question "how much does SPH particle resolution change the answer?" Both surfaces are real captured data (the development log Entries 93-99, run on the RTX 3090 machine's own local Chrono::FSI build), shown as the same smooth height-field surface the Recorded tab uses — the width-averaged density field of every real particle, read at its half-maximum crossing (see the Recorded tab's caption for why a per-cell maximum cannot work at these particle counts), then embedded as compact per-frame grids rather than raw particle positions (dx=0.005's real ~139,840-particle-per-frame capture went into computing its own grid at full density, not a visually-subsampled scatter). A useful check that this surface reconstruction isn't inventing anything: its own quality scales with the data's. At rest, where the real fluid is provably flat, the reconstructed surface is flat to 0.95 mm at dx=0.010 and 0.59 mm at dx=0.005; the fitted slope tracks tan(tank_angle) (the level-in-world condition) with correlation 0.989 at dx=0.010 and 0.998 at dx=0.005; and the apparent fluid-volume drift that forces a correction on the coarse captures (52 mm at dx=0.010) nearly vanishes at dx=0.005 (3.1 mm) — the same resolution story the numbers below tell, showing up independently in the geometry. The full-density point-cloud renders are the sph_particles_trained_seed0_dx005_publication.gif file alongside this report, if you want to see the raw particles themselves. A third, even finer real capture (dx=0.003 m, ~700,000+ particles) exists but is intentionally NOT embedded anywhere — its own raw file is 1.1 GB, bigger than GitHub's entire free Git LFS quota by itself, so it stays local-only on the RTX 3090 machine (a real, deliberate repo-management decision, not an oversight); its own publication-quality still/animation (sph_particles_trained_seed0_dx003_publication.png/.gif) is committed and viewable, just not this interactive embed. The real, quantitative finding driving all of this: dx=0.010 vs dx=0.005 differ by a mean 1.40 mm (max 4.16 mm) in fluid position over this trajectory, while dx=0.005 vs dx=0.003 differ by only 0.70 mm (max 0.92 mm) — the gap roughly HALVES as resolution increases, the real signature of numerical convergence, not just noise. Toggle between the two resolutions above and scrub through the same moments to see the actual difference this represents, not just read it as a table number.
